name: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
title: Autonomous Entities and AI Fiduciaries
answer: Autonomous entities are software systems, bots, smart contracts, or AI-operated legal wrappers that can take actions, enter agreements, hold assets, or make decisions with little or no human review at the moment of action. AI fiduciaries are a narrower set, where an AI system or the firm deploying it owes duties of loyalty and care to a beneficiary, as in robo-advisory, trust administration, or agent-managed property. The legal questions sit across agency law, corporate law, trust law, securities regulation, contract, and tort, because old doctrines assume a human actor with intent and capacity. The site's tracker counts 147 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which shows how often courts are now asked to apply those doctrines to software-driven conduct.

AI fiduciaries are a narrower set, where an AI system or the firm deploying it owes duties of loyalty and care to a beneficiary, as in robo-advisory, trust administration, or agent-managed property. The legal questions sit across agency law, corporate law, trust law, securities regulation, contract, and tort, because old doctrines assume a human actor with intent and capacity. The site's tracker counts 147 active AI lawsuits, 92 of them intellectual property, and 29 AI case law precedents, which shows how often courts are now asked to apply those doctrines to software-driven conduct.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: What these systems run on is both technical and legal. On the technical side there is cloud compute, model APIs, orchestration code, smart contracts, wallets, identity and access management, logging, and human oversight dashboards. On the legal side there is an entity wrapper, such as a corporation, LLC, or trust, plus agency agreements, terms of service, insurance, escrow, and compliance monitoring. The site's directory lists 732 AI tools, and many of them can be chained into an autonomous stack, but the legal wrapper is what usually determines who can be sued and who holds the assets.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by mapping each autonomous action to a legal person, a contract, and a control. Practitioners draft operating agreements, trust instruments, and agency contracts that define authority, limits, and reporting duties. They also review model behavior, test for bias and error, document decision rules, and set up human escalation paths for actions that carry legal or financial weight. The site's glossary has 686 terms, which reflects how much of this vocabulary is still being settled by regulators, courts, and standards bodies.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on provenance and control. If an autonomous entity holds or moves assets, the key questions are who owns the output, who has data rights, who bears loss, and whether the entity has enough capital to answer a judgment. Provenance matters because audit trails, model lineage, data sources, and decision logs are often the only way to show what happened and who was responsible. The site's compliance and regulation pages, 215 in total, track how different jurisdictions are approaching disclosure, registration, and liability for automated decision systems.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward more registration, disclosure, and insurance for autonomous systems that act in the world. The site tracks 6946 state AI bills, and many of them address automated decision systems, which will shape what an autonomous entity can legally do and what an AI fiduciary must document. Courts are still early, with 29 AI case law precedents, so the boundaries of liability, personhood, and fiduciary duty remain unsettled. Over time, expect clearer rules on human oversight, capital requirements, and audit rights, though the pace will vary by jurisdiction and by sector.
